meeting_header:
Date: 2027-11-02
Time: 15:00 - 15:48 PST
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood Solutions), Lena Ortiz (OrbitWorks CTO), Devon Park (OrbitWorks Platform Eng), Aria Singh (OrbitWorks Data Scientist), Samir Bose (OrbitWorks Security)
summary: Initial integration discovery: OrbitWorks evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private Redwood deployment for a LangChain-driven retrieval + generation product. Key concerns: latency SLOs, rate limits/quotas, gateway/proxy architecture with existing API gateway, LangChain/LlamaIndex connector patterns, observability hooks and cost tradeoffs. Action items defined for pricing, POC kickoff, and sample workload sharing.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
Gateway / proxy vs direct SDK integration
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. We're excited to talk through how Redwood would fit into OrbitWorks' stack.
[00:07] Lena (CTO): Thanks, Maya. Quick intros — I'm Lena, CTO, and I'll mostly be listening for architecture and security implications. Devon will cover infra, Aria on ML, Samir on security.
[00:16] Devon (Platform Eng): Hey all. We're looking to replace a brittle proxy we built that routes requests to a few hosted endpoints. Looking for something more predictable for latency and cost.
[00:24] Maya (AE): Totally. High-level we support Hosted API for easy onboarding, Dedicated reserved capacity for predictable throughput, and Private (VPC / on-prem) for locked-down deployments. Today let's focus on integration patterns — SDKs, LangChain, gateway/proxy, rate-limits and observability.
[00:38] Ethan (SE): Quick question—what's your expected qps and typical prompt length? That drives batching and throughput choices.
[00:45] Aria (Data Scientist): For the production intent, we get about 50 rps peak across services, average prompt is ~850 tokens when you include retrieved context, tail can spike to 120 rps for short bursts. Latency target is 300ms 95th for the summarization route, generator routes can tolerate up to 700ms.
[01:05] Maya (AE): Great, that's actionable. Devon, what gateway are you using now?
[01:09] Devon: We run Kong at the edge, and an internal sidecar that normalizes requests into a single payload for the model. Ideally we don't want to rip out Kong.
[01:17] Ethan (SE): That's fine — you can keep Kong as the edge, and either call Redwood's hosted endpoints directly from your sidecar or put a lightweight proxy that multiplexes requests and handles retries. We also have an SDK that plugs into common frameworks.
[01:29] Lena: For compliance, Samir wants to know about audit logs and who can see tokens.
[01:33] Samir (Security): Yeah, we need KMS-based encryption of logs, retained for 90 days, SOC2 report, and RBAC. Also curious if PII redaction at rest is supported.
[01:43] Maya: We have SOC2 Type II and can integrate with customer KMS in Dedicated and Private deployments. Hosted also supports most features but Dedicated/Private give you more control over key management and network egress.
[01:55] Ethan: On audit logs — we emit per-request metadata, token counts, latencies, error traces. For hosted customers we retain logs per plan; with Dedicated you can push logs to your SIEM via secure forwarder or keep them in your VPC for Private. PII redaction is something we recommend to do client-side pre-ingest, but we can also provide redaction hooks in the pipeline.
[02:15] Devon: How intrusive is the SDK? We prefer not to add heavy runtime dependencies in the sidecar.
[02:20] Ethan: Our SDK is lightweight — a small HTTP client with retry/backoff, batching helpers and native LangChain connectors. If you already have a sidecar doing normalization you can call the SDK from there, or call the REST API directly.
[02:32] Aria: Can you talk about LangChain and LlamaIndex connectors? We use LangChain extensively in our retrieval pipeline.
[02:37] Ethan: Sure. We provide an official LangChain wrapper that implements the LLM chain interface plus a retriever adapter for LlamaIndex formats. We also have a sample repo showing recommended prompt templates, caching patterns, and how to stream results back to clients.
[02:51] Devon: Streaming — is it server-sent events? Websocket? We may want to stream partial tokens to reduce perceived latency.
[02:57] Maya: Hosted API supports streaming chunked responses and you can get partial tokens. For Dedicated we've got optimized streaming with lower overhead. Private supports streaming depending on your network config.
[03:08] Lena: Rate limits are key — we have lots of internal teams with different quotas. How granular are your quotas?
[03:14] Ethan: Quotas can be token-level, route-level, or key-level. You can configure per-team API keys, rate limits per route, and burst windows. For Dedicated we can set guaranteed throughput and a burst bucket for spiky usage.
[03:26] Devon: What's the unit for quota? Tokens, requests, or both?
[03:29] Maya: Both — you can choose requests-per-second and tokens-per-minute. We show token-level cost in the console so teams can attribute spend.
[03:37] Aria: Curious about prefix/KV caching — that could save a lot for our retrieval steps.
[03:42] Ethan: We support KV cache and prefix caching. If you have a lot of repeated context, you can cache the KV cache per conversation and avoid recomputing attention states. That reduces both latency and cost.
[03:53] Samir: For Private, does the control plane see queries? We need to know about metadata and telemetry flow.
[03:58] Maya: In Private deployments the control plane is minimal and can be configured to avoid routing content. We can also deploy a completely air-gapped control plane in some enterprise agreements. Hosted obviously processes metadata for routing and observability, but you can opt out of content retention.
[04:13] Devon: Let's dig into gateway/proxy patterns — what's recommended for a company that already has an API gateway and sidecars?
[04:20] Ethan: Two patterns: 1) Gateway-forward: keep your Kong in front and have it route to Redwood endpoints per route, handle auth/ratelimit at Kong, and let Redwood handle model-level routing and batching. 2) Proxy-adapter: run a lightweight Redwood proxy or sidecar that handles batching, KV/cache, and observability, with Kong forwarding to that adapter. Pattern 2 gives better aggregation and batching, lower token cost, but you add an extra runtime component.
[04:45] Devon: We probably prefer pattern 1 to minimize infra changes unless there's a clear ROI. What's the ROI threshold?
[04:51] Ethan: If your average request length and concurrency allow batching gains of 20-40%, that usually pays for the proxy. We can run a benchmark — Redwood will replay a representative set of requests and show latency/cost delta between direct and proxy modes.
[05:05] Aria: Benchmarks — will you run them or do we?
[05:09] Maya: We'll run an initial Redwood-executed baseline if you provide the sample workload and prompts, then a joint POC where you run in your environment.
[05:17] Lena: About LangChain — we have custom tools and function-calling patterns. How do you support tool calling and structured outputs?
[05:25] Ethan: We support function/tool calling primitives and structured JSON output modes. The SDK includes helpers to wire LangChain tools into Redwood's function call interface. We do recommend using explicit output schemas to make evals and regressions easier.
[05:38] Devon: Observability hooks — can we get distributed traces correlating gateway requests to token-level traces?
[05:43] Ethan: Yes — we emit trace IDs and per-token timing. You can forward these to Jaeger/Datadog. The console will show trace breakdowns per request, token-level cost, and heatmap of sequence length distribution.
[05:58] Samir: Any pitfalls with embeddings or vector stores? We already use a hosted vector DB.
[06:03] Aria: We use LlamaIndex with Pinecone right now. Embedding throughput matters for batch updates.
[06:09] Ethan: For embeddings we can scale horizontally; embeddings can be separate endpoints or co-located with generation depending on latency needs. For batch upserts, we recommend a Dedicated pool to avoid noisy neighbor effects.
[06:21] Devon: Security — how does SSO/SAML and RBAC work?
[06:25] Maya: We support SSO/SAML and SCIM for user sync. RBAC is role-based at the org level and can be integrated with your IdP. For Dedicated and Private, you can enforce IP allowlists and custom roles.
[06:36] Samir: KMS integration specifics? We need AWS KMS in our VPC and HSM capability for a few keys.
[06:42] Ethan: Dedicated and Private support customer-managed keys via AWS KMS. HSM-backed keys can be configured for Private on-prem routes; we'll include the exact architecture in the security packet.
[06:55] Devon: A bit about model variants — what happens when capacity is constrained? Do you fall back to smaller models?
[07:01] Maya: Smart routing lets us fallback to compatible model variants (e.g., quantized or smaller architecture) according to routing policies you configure. We can also do region fallback. Rollbacks and canary deploys are supported so you can test smaller models on a fraction of traffic.
[07:15] Aria: For our evaluation, we want to try a 2-week POC using our LangChain flows against Redwood Dedicated. What would success criteria look like?
[07:23] Maya: Typical success criteria: 1) Meet latency SLOs (95th < 300ms) for the summarization route, 2) End-to-end cost per generated token below threshold you set, 3) Integrations work with existing Kong sidecar and LangChain without major code changes, 4) Observability provides actionable traces for regression alerts.
[07:40] Devon: If we go Dedicated, what's the commit? Monthly? Annual?
[07:45] Maya: We offer monthly reserved capacity or annual discounts. For Dedicated there are baseline vGPU pools with optional burst capacity; pricing depends on instance type and commit term. We'll send a pricing sheet.
[07:57] Samir: Data residency — we need EU-only for a subset of traffic. Is region routing supported?
[08:02] Ethan: Yes, you can route by region. For Hosted we have EU regions and you can pin models/traffic accordingly. For Dedicated we can provision capacity in a specific region; Private gives you full control.
[08:12] Lena: Any known gotchas with LangChain connector compatibility?
[08:15] Ethan: Mostly around streaming and tokenization differences. LangChain expects streaming iterables, so ensure you use the SDK's stream wrapper. LlamaIndex may need a small adapter for metadata passing. We have example adapters in the sample repo.
[08:29] Aria: Prompt evaluation and regression alerts — how does Redwood handle that?
[08:33] Maya: Redwood Optimize ties evals to rollout policies. You can run prompt sets against model versions and configure alerts if a metric degrades. We also surface quality regressions tied to prompts.
[08:45] Devon: Ok let's talk about quotas again — can we have per-team token budgets with automatic throttling and escalation?
[08:52] Ethan: Yes, per-team token budgets with webhooks for when thresholds are hit. You can also set automatic throttles or soft caps.
[08:59] Lena: On-call — if latency spikes in production, who do we contact?
[09:03] Maya: For Dedicated customers we provide an SLA with prioritized support and runbooks. We also have an emergency Slack channel and pager for urgent incidents.
[09:11] Aria: We have an ML concern: KV cache invalidation when context updates — how do you recommend handling conversation-aware caches?
[09:19] Ethan: We recommend per-conversation KV namespaces with TTL and explicit invalidation on writes. The SDK exposes invalidation APIs so your sidecar or LangChain wrapper can trigger it after updates.
[09:32] Devon: Let's call out the experimental things — quantization/INT8 support for cost reduction — is that production-ready?
[09:38] Ethan: We have quantized model variants that are suitable for production on certain workloads. For safety/quality you should run evals — quantized models can have subtle differences; we usually test on your prompt set during a POC.
[09:49] Samir: We need to review the security packet before any POC.
[09:52] Maya: Absolutely — we'll send the security + SOC2 + KMS docs after this call.
[09:58] (short silence)
[10:02] Lena: Is there anything around cost attribution per route? We need to bill internal teams.
[10:07] Ethan: The Console provides token & cost breakdown by API key and route, and you can export nightly CSVs to your billing system.
[10:14] Devon: Any sample rates for token-based pricing?
[10:18] Maya: We'll include tiered examples in the pricing sheet, including Dedicated committed rates and burst pricing.
[10:24] Aria: For the POC, can we get an example LangChain repo with your recommended caching pattern and a Kong config snippet?
[10:30] Ethan: Yes — we'll push a sample repo and a Kong policy example.
[10:34] Lena: Anything else we should know about latency tuning?
[10:38] Ethan: Sequence length distribution matters—short sequences benefit more from batching; long sequences can be slowed by attention operations. We'll analyze your distribution in the baseline. Also network jitter from edge to region is often the largest contributor — colocating Dedicated in the nearest region helps.
[10:54] Devon: On the fallback behavior — if a model is unavailable, will Redwood retry automatically to a smaller model?
[10:59] Maya: You can configure automatic fallback with either silent downgrade or explicit error. We default to a policy that attempts a compatible model once then reports metric.
[11:10] (overlap) Aria: Quick note — any limits on prompt size?
[11:13] Ethan: Limits depend on model; we enforce model-specific context windows. For larger contexts we recommend chunking and retrieval augmentation.
[11:19] Lena: Recap and next steps?
[11:22] Maya: Recap — Redwood will: 1) share pricing and Dedicated config examples (Maya), 2) send security packet including KMS integration and SOC2 (Maya), 3) Ethan will share LangChain/LlamaIndex sample repo and Kong snippet, 4) OrbitWorks to share sample workload and prompt set (Devon), 5) Redwood to run initial baseline and propose POC plan to start week of 11/15.
[11:47] Devon: Sounds good. We'll aim to get the workload to you by 11/05.
[11:51] Lena: We'll review the security docs once they're in.
[11:54] Maya: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the packet and a calendar invite for the POC planning.
[11:59] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard terms (K-V cash -> KV cache) and speaker labels auto-assigned; some timestamps approximate.
